questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the office with 3 weeks of fatigue, decreased activity, and easy bruising. Examination shows pallor and scattered petechiae. A complete blood count reveals an elevated white blood cell count, low hemoglobin, and a very low platelet count. A peripheral blood smear shows numerous lymphoblasts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute myeloid leukemia with Auer rods

explanation.summary: A child with cytopenias and circulating lymphoblasts has acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma until proven otherwise.
explanation.whyCorrect: In ALL, malignant lymphoblasts proliferate in and replace the marrow, crowding out normal precursors and producing anemia and thrombocytopenia while lymphoblasts spill into the blood. ALL is the most common childhood malignancy, so a child presenting with an acute leukemia is assumed to have ALL until proven otherwise.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute myeloid leukemia produces myeloblasts (often with Auer rods) rather than lymphoblasts and is far less common in children.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow and does not produce circulating blasts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura causes isolated thrombocytopenia without anemia or circulating blasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Infectious mononucleosis produces reactive atypical lymphocytes, which are mature cells, not lymphoblasts.

questions.stem: A pediatrician explains that a child who presents with an acute leukemia should be assumed to have a particular disease until proven otherwise, and that this disease is also the most common malignancy of childhood, accounting for about 25% of childhood cancers. Which of the following is this disease?

explanation.summary: ALL is the most common malignancy of childhood and the default assumption for a child with acute leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALL is much more common in children than adults and is the most common childhood malignancy overall (about 40 cases per million children), accounting for roughly 25% of childhood cancers. In children it also carries a good prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute myeloid leukemia occurs in children but is much less common than ALL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic myeloid leukemia is largely an adult disease and is rare in children.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hodgkin lymphoma typically affects older adolescents and adults and is not the most common childhood malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neuroblastoma is a common childhood solid tumor but is not a leukemia and is not the most common childhood malignancy overall.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with cough, dyspnea, and facial swelling. A chest radiograph reveals a large anterior mediastinal mass. A complete blood count shows lymphoblasts, and biopsy confirms a lymphoblastic malignancy whose cells express CD2, CD3, and CD7. Which of the following is the most likely subtype?

explanation.summary: T-cell ALL commonly presents as an anterior mediastinal mass and expresses T-cell markers such as CD2, CD3, and CD7.
explanation.whyCorrect: T-cell ALL frequently presents with lymph node or mediastinal involvement, and an anterior mediastinal mass can cause cardiorespiratory compromise. T-cell ALL is usually positive for CD2, CD3, CD4, CD7, and CD8, matching this immunophenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B-cell ALL is usually positive for CD19, CD22, and CD79a and is less associated with a mediastinal mass.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia is a myeloid disorder and does not present as a lymphoblastic mediastinal mass.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Follicular lymphoma is a mature B-cell lymphoma of adults, not a lymphoblastic malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hodgkin lymphoma is characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells, not lymphoblasts expressing TdT and T-cell CD markers.

questions.stem: A pathologist reviews marrow blasts from a newly diagnosed acute leukemia. The cells show fine chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and scant bluish cytoplasm, and no Auer rods are identified. Absence of Auer rods is most useful in distinguishing this leukemia from which of the following?

explanation.summary: Auer rods are seen in myeloblasts of acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome but not in the lymphoblasts of ALL.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike the myeloblasts of acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome, ALL lymphoblasts do not contain Auer rods (crystalline cytoplasmic inclusions). Their absence therefore helps distinguish ALL from a myeloid leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Follicular lymphoma is a mature B-cell lymphoma and is not evaluated by the presence of Auer rods.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is not a blastic malignancy, so Auer rods are not part of its differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm and does not present with Auer rod-containing blasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Auer rods do not distinguish B-cell from T-cell ALL because lymphoblasts of both subtypes lack them.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukemia is found on cytogenetic testing to have the t(9;22) translocation (Philadelphia chromosome). Addition of which of the following agents to his chemotherapy regimen is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL is treated with the addition of a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as dasatinib.
explanation.whyCorrect: The t(9;22) translocation produces the BCR-ABL fusion gene and its constitutively active tyrosine kinase. In Ph-positive ALL a tyrosine kinase inhibitor is added, and long-term dasatinib-based therapy has shown better outcomes than imatinib.

whyWrongByChoice.B: L-asparaginase is a standard chemotherapeutic and has no relation to the Philadelphia chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prednisone is a glucocorticoid backbone agent and does not specifically target the t(9;22) kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rasburicase is used to treat hyperuricemia in tumor lysis syndrome, not to target BCR-ABL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine is a standard component of induction but is not targeted to the BCR-ABL kinase.

questions.stem: A child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia and a high white blood cell count is about to begin induction chemotherapy. To prevent uric acid precipitation in the renal tubules and resulting acute renal failure, which of the following is the most appropriate prophylaxis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Packed red blood cell transfusion daily

explanation.summary: IV hydration and allopurinol are given to prevent tumor lysis syndrome and its uric acid nephropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor lysis syndrome releases potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids that are catabolized to uric acid, which can precipitate in the renal tubules and cause acute renal failure. IV hydration and allopurinol, which blocks uric acid production, are given to prevent this.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Broad-spectrum antibiotics treat infection, which does not prevent uric acid precipitation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intrathecal methotrexate is given for CNS prophylaxis, not for tumor lysis syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Packed red blood cells correct anemia and have no role in preventing tumor lysis syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet transfusion addresses thrombocytopenic bleeding, not uric acid nephropathy.

questions.stem: A patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia develops tumor lysis syndrome and has a markedly elevated uric acid level despite allopurinol. Rasburicase is administered. Rasburicase lowers the uric acid level by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking xanthine oxidase to reduce uric acid production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing renal reabsorption of uric acid

explanation.summary: Rasburicase is a recombinant urate-oxidase enzyme that converts existing uric acid to allantoin.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the uric acid level is already elevated, rasburicase is administered. It is a recombinant urate-oxidase enzyme that converts uric acid to allantoin, an inactive and soluble metabolite, thereby lowering the existing uric acid burden.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Urinary alkalinization is a separate supportive measure and is not how rasburicase acts.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking xanthine oxidase to reduce uric acid production describes allopurinol, which prevents formation rather than degrading existing uric acid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rasburicase lowers uric acid; it does not increase its renal reabsorption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting purine synthesis is not the mechanism of rasburicase.

questions.stem: One agent in a pediatric ALL induction regimen is an enzyme derived from bacteria that deprives leukemic cells of an amino acid they are unable to synthesize because they lack the necessary synthetase. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this agent?

explanation.summary: Asparaginase depletes circulating asparagine, starving leukemic cells that cannot synthesize it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Asparaginase catalyzes conversion of L-asparagine into aspartic acid and ammonia, reducing circulating asparagine. Leukemic cells lack asparagine synthetase activity and cannot make their own, so depriving them of an exogenous source leads to cell death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cross-linking DNA describes an alkylating agent such as cyclophosphamide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase describes tyrosine kinase inhibitors used in Ph-positive ALL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase is the mechanism of methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting microtubule assembly is the mechanism of vincristine, not asparaginase.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old receiving induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia develops paresthesias, loss of deep tendon reflexes, and constipation. Which chemotherapeutic agent, acting by inhibition of microtubule function, is most likely responsible for these findings?

explanation.summary: Vincristine inhibits microtubule function and causes dose-related peripheral neuropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vincristine acts by inhibition of microtubule function, and its use is associated with dose-related peripheral neuropathy that can cause paresthesia, loss of reflexes, weakness, and autonomic effects including vocal cord paralysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytarabine causes myelosuppression and megaloblastic anemia, not this neuropathic pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Daunorubicin inhibits DNA/RNA synthesis and causes cumulative cardiomyopathy, not peripheral neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L-asparaginase causes pancreatitis, coagulopathy, and hepatic toxicity rather than neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prednisone causes steroid-associated effects such as fractures and mood changes, not peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: Prior to starting systemic therapy, a child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia undergoes a lumbar puncture through which chemotherapy is delivered into the subarachnoid space. What is the primary rationale for delivering chemotherapy by this route?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The CNS is a sanctuary site

choices.label: D
choices.text: To obtain a bone marrow sample

explanation.summary: Intrathecal chemotherapy is used because the CNS is a sanctuary site with barriers that resist systemic chemotherapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALL has a high propensity to disseminate to the CNS, which is concerning because the CNS has built-in barriers that make it resistant to some systemic chemotherapy. Intrathecal chemotherapy delivered into the subarachnoid space, along with prophylactic dosing, targets this sanctuary site.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperuricemia is managed with hydration, allopurinol, or rasburicase, not intrathecal therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mediastinal disease is evaluated with imaging such as a chest radiograph, not a lumbar puncture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A bone marrow sample is obtained by bone marrow biopsy/aspirate, not by intrathecal drug delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombocytopenic bleeding is managed with platelet support, not intrathecal chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A teenager treated for acute lymphoblastic leukemia is monitored for cumulative dose-related cardiac toxicity during therapy. Which agent in the induction regimen is most associated with cardiomyopathy?

explanation.summary: Daunorubicin causes cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy that can progress to heart failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Daunorubicin inhibits DNA/RNA synthesis, and its characteristic toxicity is cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy, which can also lead to heart failure, so cardiac function is monitored during therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytarabine causes myelosuppression and megaloblastic anemia rather than cardiomyopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L-asparaginase causes pancreatitis, coagulopathy, and hepatic toxicity rather than cardiac toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate causes myelosuppression, nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, and mucositis, not cardiomyopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy, not cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry of a child's marrow blasts shows expression of CD19, CD22, and CD79a, and the nuclear enzyme terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is positive. These findings best support which of the following diagnoses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid markers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia, a mature B-cell tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multiple myeloma, a plasma cell neoplasm

explanation.summary: CD19, CD22, and CD79a with nuclear TdT positivity identify B-cell ALL.
explanation.whyCorrect: B-cell ALL is usually positive for CD19, CD22, and CD79a. TdT is expressed in the nucleus of lymphoblasts and disappears as the cell matures, so its presence supports a lymphoblastic malignancy; together these findings indicate B-cell ALL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute myeloid leukemia expresses myeloid markers and does not express this B-lymphoid, TdT-positive profile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a mature B-cell disorder and is TdT negative.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm and does not express a TdT-positive lymphoblast profile.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T-cell ALL is usually positive for CD2, CD3, CD4, CD7, and CD8 rather than the B-cell markers shown.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis is hospitalized for a flare and treated with high-dose corticosteroids. She now feels well, and her temperature has been normal throughout admission with an unremarkable physical examination. Morning laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 16,000/mm3 with 92% mature segmented neutrophils. Which of the following best explains her elevated neutrophil count?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Occult bacterial infection with left shift

explanation.summary: Corticosteroids cause a benign mature neutrophilia by driving marginated neutrophils into the circulating pool (demargination).
explanation.whyCorrect: In the absence of signs or symptoms of infection, an elevated count of mature segmented neutrophils in a patient on high-dose steroids reflects benign leukocytosis. Steroids and stress cause marginated neutrophils pressed against the vessel wall to enter the bloodstream, a process called demargination; because roughly half of the body's neutrophils are normally marginated, this can significantly raise the count without any increase in marrow production. It is not a serious concern and requires no further testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia produces circulating lymphoblasts with dangerously low normal WBCs, not a predominance of mature neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia typically produces a markedly high WBC count and is often accompanied by basophilia, not a modest steroid-associated rise in mature neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A leukoerythroblastic reaction shows immature neutrophils and nucleated red blood cells, which are not present here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There are no signs or symptoms of infection by history or physical examination, and the cells are all mature without a left shift.

questions.stem: A hematologist defines a laboratory finding as an elevated white blood cell count in the peripheral blood, greater than 11,000 cells/mm3, that is caused by something other than a neoplasm. Which of the following terms best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: Benign leukocytosis is an elevated peripheral WBC count (>11,000/mm3) caused by something other than neoplasms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leukocytosis means the WBC count is above the normal range; benign leukocytosis specifically denotes an elevation greater than 11,000 cells/mm3 that is not due to a hematopoietic neoplasm. The most common cause is infection, and other causes include drugs, inflammatory diseases, and stress.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A leukoerythroblastic reaction is one specific pattern of immature neutrophilia, not the general term for a non-neoplastic elevated count.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leukopenia is a decreased WBC count, the opposite of leukocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neoplastic leukocytosis is caused by bone marrow neoplasms and is often associated with very high WBC counts of 100,000/mm3 or more.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutropenia refers to a depletion of neutrophils, not an elevated total WBC count.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with fever, sweating, and fatigue. Her complete blood count shows a WBC count of 18,000/mm3 with 60% neutrophils. The blood smear reveals occasional bands, metamyelocytes, and promyelocytes, along with many mature segmented neutrophils containing dark cytoplasmic granules. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her findings?

explanation.summary: Neutrophilia with a left shift and toxic granulation is characteristic of a leukemoid reaction to bacterial infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has neutrophilia with a left shift (immature neutrophil forms such as bands, metamyelocytes, and promyelocytes), characteristic of a leukemoid reaction due to infection or inflammation. The dark granules represent toxic granulation, which is most consistent with a bacterial infection and accounts for her fever.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute leukemia would show numerous circulating blast cells rather than a maturing left shift with toxic granulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia typically shows a markedly high WBC count, usually more than 100,000/mm3.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parasitic infection is typically associated with eosinophilia, not neutrophilia with toxic changes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reactive lymphocytosis involves a proliferation of reactive lymphocytes, not neutrophils with a left shift.

questions.stem: A patient admitted to the hospital has a blood smear showing a left shift. Which of the following cell types is most likely to be present in increased numbers?

explanation.summary: A left shift refers to the presence of immature neutrophils (bands, metamyelocytes, promyelocytes) in the peripheral blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally only mature segmented neutrophils are seen in the blood. A left shift means neutrophil precursors are present in the circulation, most commonly as a response to infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophils are elevated in allergies, myeloproliferative disorders, hypothyroidism, and certain infections, not in a left shift.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophils are elevated in allergies, drug reactions, asthma, and parasitic worm infections.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monocytes are occasionally elevated in conditions such as chronic infection or inflammation but do not define a left shift.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactive lymphocytes are seen primarily in viral infections, not in a neutrophil left shift.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic patient has a routine complete blood count showing a total leukocyte count of 10,000 cells/mm3. The differential shows 50% neutrophils, 45% lymphocytes, 3% monocytes, 1% eosinophils, and 1% basophils. The blood smear reveals normal-appearing cells. Which of the following disorders is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: A normal total WBC count with an elevated absolute lymphocyte count (>4000/mm3) indicates lymphocytosis, and normal-appearing cells make it a non-reactive lymphocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The total leukocyte count is normal at 10,000/mm3, but 45% lymphocytes yields an absolute lymphocyte count of 4500, above the normal upper limit of about 4000. This is lymphocytosis. Because the cells appear normal under the microscope, it is not a reactive lymphocytosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The absolute neutrophil count (5000) is normal (below 7700), so immature neutrophilia is not present.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The absolute neutrophil count is normal, so mature neutrophilia is not present either.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The monocyte count is normal, making monocytosis incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactive lymphocytosis would show abnormal reactive lymphocyte forms, whereas the cells here appear normal.

questions.stem: A neutrophil on a blood smear from a septic patient contains numerous small, clear, membrane-bound bubbles in its cytoplasm. This toxic change occurs by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Degranulation of lysosomes within the neutrophil

choices.label: C
choices.text: Demargination of neutrophils from the vessel wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of nucleated red blood cells from the marrow

explanation.summary: Cytoplasmic vacuolization results from degranulation of lysosomes within neutrophils and is typically seen in sepsis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A vacuole is a membrane-bound vesicle in the cytoplasm. Cytoplasmic vacuolization occurs due to degranulation of lysosomes within the neutrophils, appearing as small clear bubbles. The process usually occurs in cases of sepsis, when there is widespread destruction of pathogens inside the neutrophils.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum remnants describe Dohle bodies, not vacuolization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Demargination raises the mature neutrophil count but does not create cytoplasmic vacuoles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased primary granules containing peroxidases and hydrolases describe toxic granulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Release of nucleated red blood cells is characteristic of a leukoerythroblastic reaction, not vacuolization.

questions.stem: A blood smear from a patient with a bacterial infection shows neutrophils containing small blue-gray oval inclusions located at the periphery of the cytoplasm. These inclusions are composed of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crystalline aggregates of fused azurophilic granules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fragments of nucleated red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peroxidases and hydrolases within primary granules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ribosomes and remnants of rough endoplasmic reticulum

explanation.summary: Dohle bodies are blue-gray peripheral cytoplasmic inclusions made of ribosomes and remnants of rough endoplasmic reticulum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dohle bodies are small circular or oval blue-gray cytoplasmic inclusions usually located at the periphery of the neutrophil. They consist of ribosomes and remnants of rough endoplasmic reticulum and are often a manifestation of the increased protein production in neutrophils responding to a bacterial infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crystalline granule aggregates (Auer rods) are seen in myeloid blasts, not as Dohle bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nucleated red blood cell fragments are not the composition of Dohle bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Membrane-bound vesicles from lysosomal degranulation describe cytoplasmic vacuolization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peroxidases and hydrolases in primary granules describe toxic granulation, not Dohle bodies.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student presents with fever, sore throat, and cervical lymphadenopathy. A blood smear shows an increased number of large lymphocytes with abundant, agranular cytoplasm and a fried-egg appearance that molds around adjacent red blood cells. These cells are most characteristic of infection with which of the following?

explanation.summary: Downey type II reactive lymphocytes are most commonly associated with Epstein-Barr virus (infectious mononucleosis).
explanation.whyCorrect: Downey cells are a specific type of reactive lymphocyte. Downey type II cells are the most common type and are often associated with Epstein-Barr virus. They are larger cells, often with a fried-egg appearance, and have abundant agranular cytoplasm that abuts or molds around adjacent erythrocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bordetella pertussis causes lymphocytosis with normal-appearing lymphocytes, not reactive Downey cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coxsackievirus causes infectious lymphocytosis with normal-appearing lymphocytes, typically in children.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause lymphocytosis but is not the classic cause of Downey type II cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Staphylococcus aureus causes a neutrophilic response with toxic changes, not reactive lymphocytosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with a history of asthma and seasonal allergies is evaluated for an elevated white blood cell count, and his differential shows an increased eosinophil count. Besides allergies, asthma, and drug reactions, which of the following is most classically associated with eosinophilia?

explanation.summary: Eosinophilia (>500/mm3) is classically associated with allergies, drug reactions, asthma, and helminthic (parasitic worm) infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: An elevated eosinophil count is fairly common and is associated with many conditions, including allergies, drug reactions, asthma, and helminthic (parasitic worm) infections. Of the options, parasitic worm infection is the classic infectious cause of eosinophilia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacterial infection classically causes neutrophilia, not eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute stress causes neutrophilia via demargination or a transient lymphocytosis, not eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Viral infection classically raises the lymphocyte count.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypothyroidism is a classic cause of basophilia, not eosinophilia.

questions.stem: A previously healthy man is found to have persistent basophilia on repeated complete blood counts, with no evidence of allergy, hypothyroidism, or recent infection. This finding is classically associated with which of the following neoplastic disorders?

explanation.summary: Basophilia is the least common benign leukocytosis but is classically seen in myeloproliferative disorders, particularly chronic myeloid leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Basophilia (>300/mm3) is the least common type of benign leukocytosis, with benign causes including allergies, hypothyroidism, and certain infections. There are also neoplastic diseases (myeloproliferative disorders) that classically show basophilia, particularly chronic myeloid leukemia and, to a lesser extent, polycythemia vera.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia produces circulating lymphoblasts, not a characteristic basophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Follicular lymphoma is a mature B-cell lymphoma and is not associated with basophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Infectious mononucleosis causes a reactive lymphocytosis, not basophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm and does not classically cause basophilia.

questions.stem: A patient with severe anemia has a blood smear showing both immature neutrophils and nucleated (immature) red blood cells in the peripheral blood. Which of the following best describes this pattern of benign immature neutrophilia?

explanation.summary: A leukoerythroblastic reaction is defined by immature neutrophils together with nucleated red blood cells in the peripheral blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a leukoerythroblastic reaction (sometimes called a myelophthisic process), there are two kinds of immature cells in the blood: immature neutrophils and immature (nucleated) red blood cells. This can represent a normal bone marrow response, most often in severe anemia when the marrow is operating at high speed, but it can also occur when a neoplasm or fibrosis fills the marrow so cells leave early.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A leukemoid reaction includes immature neutrophils and their precursors but not nucleated red blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Benign mature neutrophilia shows only normal mature segmented neutrophils, with no immature forms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Demargination shifts existing mature neutrophils into the circulation and does not release nucleated red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactive lymphocytosis involves reactive lymphocytes, not immature neutrophils and nucleated red cells.

questions.stem: A clinician notes that in most conditions, relying only on differential percentages can be misleading, and that a particular value is generally most important in diagnosing conditions. Which of the following is generally most important?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The absolute counts of the individual WBC types

choices.label: B
choices.text: The morphology of the red blood cells on the smear

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ratio of neutrophils to lymphocytes reported

choices.label: D
choices.text: The relative percentages of the individual WBC types

choices.label: E
choices.text: The total WBC count without the differential

explanation.summary: Absolute counts, not percentages, are generally most important in diagnosing most conditions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although differential percentages are important and easy to use, they can sometimes lead you astray if you do not pay attention to the absolute values. In general, the absolute counts, not the percentages, are most important in diagnosing most conditions. The absolute count is obtained by multiplying the total WBC count by the percentage of each type.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Red blood cell morphology is not the WBC value used to interpret the differential.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio is not the value the brick emphasizes for diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Percentages alone can be misleading because a normal percentage can correspond to an abnormal absolute number and vice versa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The total WBC count alone does not reveal which specific cell line is increased or decreased.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is evaluated for a neck mass. On examination, several enlarged cervical lymph nodes are palpated. Which of the following physical findings would most strongly suggest a benign, rather than neoplastic, cause of her lymphadenopathy?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nodes that are firm and rubbery-hard

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nodes that are fixed to the underlying tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nodes that are immobile on palpation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nodes that are soft, freely movable, and tender

explanation.summary: Benign lymphadenopathy typically produces nodes that are soft, smooth, freely movable, and often tender.
explanation.whyCorrect: In benign lymphadenopathy, nodes are generally soft, smooth, freely moveable, and often tender because the enlargement results from reactive hyperplasia rather than infiltrative growth. Neoplastic nodes, by contrast, tend to be firm, immobile, fixed to the underlying tissue, and painless.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Painless nodes are typical of malignancy; benign reactive nodes are often tender.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Firm, hard nodes are characteristic of neoplastic rather than benign lymphadenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fixation to underlying tissue is a feature that favors a neoplastic process, not a benign one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immobility suggests infiltration by tumor and points away from a benign cause.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is found to have an enlarged, firm lymph node just above the left clavicle. It is nontender and fixed. Enlargement of this particular node should most prompt a search for a malignancy in which of the following locations?

explanation.summary: The left supraclavicular (Virchow) node drains the abdomen and its enlargement suggests abdominal, especially gastric, cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: The left supraclavicular node, also called the Virchow node, receives abdominal lymphatics that drain into the thoracic duct and then into the left supraclavicular node. An enlarged node here should prompt a search for an abdominal cancer, particularly gastric cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Breast cancer classically involves axillary nodes rather than the left supraclavicular node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chest malignancy such as lung cancer is suggested by an enlarged right supraclavicular node, not the left.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral and pharyngeal disease points to submandibular or submental nodes, not the supraclavicular region.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Upper extremity infection drains to axillary nodes, not to the supraclavicular area.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has a dry cough and mild fatigue. A chest radiograph shows symmetric bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Which of the following conditions is most consistent with this pattern of adenopathy?

explanation.summary: Hilar lymphadenopathy classically points to lung infection, lung cancer, or the granulomatous condition sarcoidosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hilar lymphadenopathy most often indicates a lung infection, lung cancer, or sarcoidosis, and sarcoidosis classically presents with bilateral hilar adenopathy. This granulomatous disease is a well-recognized benign cause of adenopathy in this location.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A dental abscess causes submandibular or submental adenopathy, not hilar enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric carcinoma would be suggested by a left supraclavicular (Virchow) node rather than bilateral hilar nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxoplasmosis typically causes generalized or head-and-neck adenopathy, not an isolated bilateral hilar pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Typhoid fever produces mesenteric adenopathy rather than hilar lymphadenopathy.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman develops diffuse lymph node enlargement two weeks after starting a new medication for a seizure disorder. She also has a low-grade fever and joint aches resembling serum sickness. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction most likely underlies this drug-induced generalized adenopathy?

explanation.summary: Many drugs cause generalized adenopathy through a serum-sickness-like, type 3 hypersensitivity reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The article notes that drugs most commonly cause generalized adenopathy via a serum-sickness-like hypersensitivity reaction, which is a type 3 (immune complex) hypersensitivity. Antiseizure medications such as carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and primidone are among the drugs implicated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgA-mediated mucosal reactions are not the mechanism of drug-induced generalized lymphadenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type 1 hypersensitivity mediates anaphylaxis and allergic reactions, not serum-sickness-like generalized adenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type 2 hypersensitivity involves antibody-mediated cell destruction, which is not the mechanism described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type 4 hypersensitivity is delayed and T-cell mediated, whereas the serum-sickness-like drug reaction is immune complex driven.

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy from a patient with a chronic infection shows enlarged follicles containing prominent germinal centers with tingible body macrophages. This pattern of benign follicular hyperplasia is driven predominantly by proliferation of which of the following cell types?

explanation.summary: Benign follicular hyperplasia reflects B-cell proliferation within lymph node follicles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Benign follicular hyperplasia is caused by B-cell proliferation in the lymph node follicles in response to an immune stimulus. The stimulus converts small primary follicles into enlarged secondary follicles that develop germinal centers containing proliferating lymphocytes and tingible body macrophages.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibroblasts contribute to fibrosis, not to the reactive follicular hyperplasia of an immune response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are agents of acute suppurative inflammation and are not the basis of follicular hyperplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma cells may be present but are not the proliferating population that defines follicular hyperplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T-cell proliferation drives interfollicular/paracortical hyperplasia, not follicular hyperplasia.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with a recent viral illness has a lymph node biopsy showing diffuse expansion of the paracortex and the areas between the follicles. A predominant proliferation of which of the following cell types best explains this reactive pattern?

explanation.summary: Benign interfollicular/paracortical hyperplasia represents a predominant T-cell response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Benign interfollicular/paracortical hyperplasia represents a predominant T-cell (not B-cell) response to an immune stimulus, and the lymph node shows expansion of the paracortex and the areas between follicles. Causes of this paracortical pattern include viral infection, vaccination, reaction to a nearby malignancy, and autoimmune disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B-cell proliferation produces follicular hyperplasia with germinal centers, not paracortical expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endothelial cells line vessels and are not the proliferating population in this reactive pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mast cells mediate allergic responses and do not drive paracortical hyperplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osteoclasts are bone-resorbing cells and have no role in lymph node paracortical hyperplasia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops an infected laceration on his right hand after a gardening injury. Over the next few days he notices tender swelling in the ipsilateral armpit. Enlargement of which group of lymph nodes best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: The axillary nodes drain the upper extremity and enlarge with an arm or hand infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Axillary nodes drain the upper extremities, so an infection of the hand or arm produces regional axillary adenopathy. A localized infection often presents with related regional lymphadenopathy in the nodes that drain the affected site.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hilar nodes drain the lungs and are unrelated to a hand infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The left supraclavicular node drains the abdomen and would not enlarge from a hand infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mesenteric nodes drain intra-abdominal structures and are seen with conditions such as typhoid fever.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Submental nodes drain the floor of the mouth and chin, not the upper extremity.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is evaluated for enlarged cervical lymph nodes that appeared shortly after he began atenolol for newly diagnosed hypertension. He has no fever, no weight loss, and no other findings; examination and laboratory studies show no evidence of infection or malignancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perform excisional biopsy of a cervical node now

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start anti-inflammatory therapy for an autoimmune disease

explanation.summary: Management of benign lymphadenopathy is tailored to the cause; drug-induced adenopathy resolves after stopping the offending drug.
explanation.whyCorrect: Management is tailored to the underlying cause, and treatment is based on eliminating infections, stopping offending drugs, and addressing inflammatory conditions. When the clinical picture points to a drug such as atenolol as the cause, stopping the offending drug will likely lead to resolution of the lymphadenopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics treat adenopathy secondary to infection, but no infection is identified in this case.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Systemic corticosteroids are not the initial step; removing the offending drug is the appropriate action.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Excisional biopsy is reserved for adenopathy that does not resolve with initial measures or that raises concern for malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-inflammatory therapy addresses an underlying inflammatory disorder, which is not present here.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman presents with a single, 1.5 cm, movable, rubbery lymph node in her right axilla. She has not felt any lump herself, and the rest of the examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

explanation.summary: A single enlarged axillary node in a woman warrants breast evaluation to exclude breast cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: A single enlarged axillary node suggests pathology in the arm or chest wall, and in women breast cancer is an obvious consideration because the axillary nodes drain the breast. A thorough breast exam and mammography are the appropriate next steps so that malignancy can be excluded, with biopsy reserved for later if these are unrevealing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Stopping medications is used for drug-induced adenopathy, which typically causes diffuse rather than single-node enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV testing is appropriate for unexplained generalized adenopathy, not for a single localized axillary node.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymph node biopsy would only be done after routine testing such as mammography, not as the immediate first step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reassurance without workup is inappropriate because a solitary axillary node in a woman requires exclusion of breast cancer.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has enlarged cervical lymph nodes together with a 6 kg unintentional weight loss and drenching night sweats over the past two months. On examination, a firm node is fixed to underlying tissue. Which of the following is the most appropriate step on initial workup?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prescribe a course of oral antibiotics

explanation.summary: Signs or symptoms of cancer, such as weight loss and a fixed node, warrant lymph node biopsy on initial workup.
explanation.whyCorrect: A lymph node biopsy is indicated on initial workup if the patient has underlying signs or symptoms of cancer, such as weight loss, fever, or a palpable tumor outside the nodes. The goal is to exclude neoplastic causes of the lymphadenopathy, which this patient's weight loss and fixed, firm node raise concern for.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stopping medications addresses drug-induced adenopathy and does not fit a patient with weight loss and a fixed node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A four-week period of observation is appropriate for unexplained local adenopathy without worrisome features, not for adenopathy with cancer warning signs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A heterophile test evaluates for mononucleosis and would not address the concern for malignancy raised by his systemic symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Empiric antibiotics would only be reasonable if infection were suspected, not when malignancy is the concern.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has enlargement of noncontiguous cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes without an obvious localizing source. History and physical examination do not reveal the cause. Which of the following sets of tests is the most appropriate initial evaluation for this generalized adenopathy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy as the first step

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete blood count, HIV test, and chest x-ray

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum ferritin, iron, and total iron-binding capacity

explanation.summary: Generalized adenopathy is initially evaluated with tests such as a CBC, HIV test, and chest x-ray.
explanation.whyCorrect: For generalized adenopathy, testing may include a CBC, HIV test, and chest x-ray, with testing for tuberculosis and EBV also conducted. If all of these are negative, a biopsy may then be done on an easily reached node in the neck or supraclavicular area.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone marrow biopsy is not the routine first step; initial testing screens for infection and systemic disease first.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mammography targets a single axillary node in a woman with possible breast cancer, not diffuse generalized adenopathy in a young man.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron studies evaluate anemia and are unrelated to the workup of generalized lymphadenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Upper endoscopy pursues gastric disease suggested by a Virchow node, not undifferentiated generalized adenopathy.

questions.stem: A histopathologist examines a reactive lymph node and points out large phagocytic cells within the germinal center that contain engulfed cellular debris, described as tingible body macrophages. In which region of the lymph node are these cells and their surrounding germinal center normally located?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Within the hilum near the efferent vessel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Within the paracortex among the T cells

explanation.summary: Germinal centers with tingible body macrophages reside in secondary follicles of the follicular (B-cell) region.
explanation.whyCorrect: The follicular region contains B cells arranged in follicles, and secondary follicles contain a germinal center that has been antigenically stimulated. The germinal center holds proliferating lymphocytes along with tingible body macrophages that are busy cleaning up cellular debris.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The hilum is where vessels enter and leave the node and does not contain germinal centers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The medullary cords are deep cords rich in plasma cells, not the location of germinal-center macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The paracortex is the T-cell zone that surrounds the follicles and does not house germinal centers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The subcapsular sinus is a lymphatic channel beneath the capsule, not the site of germinal centers.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old wildlife biologist presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of sudden high fever, chills, and a painful swelling in his right groin. He works outdoors in rural New Mexico and reports handling a dead prairie dog without gloves several days ago. On examination he appears acutely ill and has a tender, markedly enlarged inguinal lymph node. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent?

explanation.summary: Sudden fever with a tender bubo after rodent exposure in the western US is classic bubonic plague.
explanation.whyCorrect: Y. pestis is endemic in the western United States, where rodents, prairie dogs, and squirrels are natural reservoirs and the flea is the main vector. Bubonic plague, the most common form, follows a flea bite or contact with an infected animal or carcass and produces a massively enlarged, tender lymph node (bubo) with sudden fever and chills.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B. henselae causes milder lymphadenopathy after a cat scratch or bite, not an acute febrile bubo after rodent contact.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. trachomatis L1-L3 causes lymphogranuloma venereum, a sexually transmitted infection with buboes, not a zoonotic exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: F. tularensis typically produces an ulcer at the inoculation site and is found predominantly in the Ozarks after rabbit or tick exposure, not prairie dog handling in the western US.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Human herpesvirus-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, not an acute febrile lymphadenopathy after rodent contact.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A patient with suspected plague has an aspirate taken from an enlarged inguinal lymph node. The sample is sent for staining. Which of the following staining patterns would most strongly support a diagnosis of Yersinia pestis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gram-positive cocci arranged in long chains

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gram-positive cocci arranged in grapelike clusters

explanation.summary: Y. pestis is a gram-negative bacillus that shows a distinctive bipolar 'safety-pin' staining pattern.
explanation.whyCorrect: Y. pestis is a non-motile, gram-negative facultative anaerobe. With select stains, the dye concentrates at the ends of the bacillus, giving a bipolar appearance that resembles a safety pin. Patient samples such as bubo aspirates, blood, or sputum are examined for this pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acid-fast bacilli suggest mycobacteria; Y. pestis is not acid-fast.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gram-negative diplococci suggest organisms such as Neisseria, not the bipolar bacillus of plague.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gram-positive cocci in chains suggest Streptococcus species, not Y. pestis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gram-positive cocci in clusters suggest Staphylococcus species, not a gram-negative plague bacillus.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 40 cells/uL presents with fever and multiple red-purple, dome-shaped skin nodules on his trunk and arms that have gradually increased over the past month. The lesions are tender and bleed easily. Biopsy stain reveals small gram-negative bacilli, and histology shows neutrophilic infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent?

explanation.summary: Vascular skin nodules in a severely immunocompromised host caused by a gram-negative bacillus indicate bacillary angiomatosis from B. henselae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacillary angiomatosis is seen only in severely immunocompromised patients, such as HIV patients with T-cell counts below 100 cells/uL. It presents with multiple disseminated bright red or purple vascular skin nodules. B. henselae lesions are tender, bleed easily, and show neutrophilic infiltrates, distinguishing them from Kaposi sarcoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C. trachomatis L1-L3 causes lymphogranuloma venereum with genital ulcers and buboes, not vascular skin nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: F. tularensis causes ulceroglandular, pneumonic, or typhoidal disease, not disseminated vascular nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which resembles bacillary angiomatosis but is caused by a virus (not a gram-negative bacillus); its lesions are usually painless, do not bleed, and show lymphocytic infiltrates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Y. pestis causes plague with buboes and pneumonia, not chronic vascular skin nodules.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 45-year-old hunter in Arkansas presents with fever, chills, and a painful swollen lymph node in his right axilla. A few days earlier he skinned a wild rabbit and later noticed a small ulcer with an erythematous base on the dorsum of his right hand. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent?

explanation.summary: A skin ulcer at the inoculation site plus regional lymphadenopathy after rabbit exposure in the Ozarks is classic ulceroglandular tularemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: F. tularensis is transmitted by direct contact with rabbits or by tick and deer fly bites, and skinning a rabbit can aerosolize or inoculate the bacteria. Ulceroglandular disease is the most common form (75-85%) and uniquely causes ulceration at the inoculation site with enlarged regional lymph nodes. Most US cases occur in the Ozarks (Arkansas and Missouri).

whyWrongByChoice.A: B. henselae follows a cat scratch or bite, not rabbit skinning, and causes milder lymphadenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. trachomatis L1-L3 is sexually transmitted and causes genital ulcers, not a hand ulcer from rabbit contact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. aureus can cause skin infection and lymphadenopathy but does not fit the rabbit exposure and classic ulceroglandular pattern in an endemic area.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Y. pestis causes a bubo but classically does not ulcerate at the inoculation site and is found in the western US after rodent exposure.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: The F1 antigen capsule is an important virulence factor of Yersinia pestis. Which of the following best describes a distinguishing property of this capsule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It enhances phagocytosis of the bacterium by neutrophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is composed of lipopolysaccharide endotoxin

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is composed predominantly of protein rather than polysaccharide

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is encoded on the bacterial chromosome rather than a plasmid

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is produced at 25 degrees C within the flea vector

explanation.summary: Unlike most encapsulated bacteria, the Y. pestis capsule is protein-based, built predominantly from the F1 antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: What distinguishes the Y. pestis capsule from most other bacterial capsules is that it is protein-based, constructed predominantly from the F1 antigen (a protein), rather than the polysaccharide typical of most encapsulated bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The capsule is anti-phagocytic and conceals surface antigens, providing early immune evasion, not enhanced phagocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: LPS is a separate gram-negative endotoxin; the capsule is made from the F1 antigen protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The capsule is encoded on a plasmid, not the chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The capsule is only produced at 37 degrees C, not at the flea's 25 degrees C body temperature, allowing the bacterium to conserve energy.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is diagnosed with septicemic plague and is critically ill with hypotension and evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line antibiotic for this severe infection?

explanation.summary: Severe or systemic plague is treated first-line with an intravenous aminoglycoside such as gentamicin.
explanation.whyCorrect: For severe disease presentations such as septicemic or pneumonic plague, the first-line therapy is intravenous aminoglycosides, typically gentamicin, which provide reliable bactericidal activity in life-threatening infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azithromycin is a first-line agent for cat scratch disease, not for severe plague.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ciprofloxacin (a fluoroquinolone) is an option for mild, stable cases, not the preferred agent for severe disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxycycline is effective for plague but is reserved for mild, non-severe cases or when other options are contraindicated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillin V is a beta-lactam that does not provide coverage against plague.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: Yersinia pestis is a facultative intracellular pathogen that can survive attacks by phagocytes in the lymph nodes. Which of the following mechanisms best explains how Y. pestis directly delivers immunosuppressive effector proteins into host phagocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A type III secretion system that injects Yops into host cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of a biofilm that physically excludes neutrophils

choices.label: C
choices.text: Production of an exotoxin that ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of coagulase that forms a protective fibrin clot

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretion of a polysaccharide capsule that lyses phagocytes

explanation.summary: Y. pestis uses a syringe-like type III secretion system to inject Yersinia outer proteins (Yops) into phagocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Yops are delivered to host cells via type III secretion systems (T3SS), transmembrane protein complexes that function like a syringe. As phagocytes approach, Y. pestis uses the T3SS to inject Yops into those cells, effectively neutralizing them, which is why the bacterium can fight the immune system from within the lymph nodes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Biofilm exclusion of neutrophils is not the described mechanism; Yops are actively injected via the T3SS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The article does not attribute plague virulence to an EF-2-inactivating exotoxin; effectors are delivered by the T3SS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Coagulase and fibrin clot formation are not the described mechanism for Yop delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The capsule is anti-phagocytic and conceals antigens, but it does not lyse phagocytes or deliver effector proteins.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A laboratory attempts to culture Francisella tularensis from a patient with suspected tularemia. Which of the following is a specific requirement for successful growth of this organism in culture?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anaerobic incubation with added vitamin K and hemin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Charcoal-yeast extract agar with iron and cysteine at 42 degrees C for Legionella

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chocolate agar supplemented with factors V and X

choices.label: D
choices.text: Media supplemented with cysteine, often charcoal agar

explanation.summary: F. tularensis culture requires cysteine, often on charcoal agar, and must be handled carefully because of its low infectious dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because infection can occur with a very small inoculum, culture of F. tularensis is dangerous and must be done with cysteine, often in charcoal agar; this is a requirement for the organism to grow. F. tularensis is a BSL3 pathogen, so labs must be alerted when it is suspected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anaerobic incubation with vitamin K and hemin is used for organisms such as Bacteroides, not F. tularensis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick specifies cysteine and charcoal agar for F. tularensis and does not describe a Legionella-specific protocol as the requirement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chocolate agar with factors V and X supports Haemophilus influenzae, not F. tularensis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tellurite agar is used for Corynebacterium diphtheriae, not tularemia.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A patient develops severe pneumonia with a productive cough and bloody sputum after close contact with another person who had plague pneumonia. Which of the following best explains why pneumonic plague, unlike pneumonic tularemia, is a major public health concern for person-to-person spread?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Once Y. pestis actively replicates in the lungs, it spreads person-to-person

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pneumonic plague is transmitted exclusively by flea bites indoors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pneumonic tularemia spreads more efficiently between people than pneumonic plague

choices.label: D
choices.text: Y. pestis is transmitted person-to-person only through contaminated blood products

choices.label: E
choices.text: Y. pestis requires an arthropod vector to move between human hosts

explanation.summary: Pneumonic plague can spread directly between people by respiratory droplets, making prompt treatment critical.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once Y. pestis is actively replicating in the lungs, it can spread person-to-person via respiratory droplets. Pneumonic plague causes severe pneumonia with necrotization of lung tissue and a productive cough with bloody sputum (hemoptysis), and prompt treatment is critical to prevent spread.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pneumonic plague is acquired by aerosolized droplets or blood spread to the lungs, not exclusively indoor flea bites.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Unlike pneumonic plague, there is no significant person-to-person transmission of tularemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transmission is via respiratory droplets from active lung infection, not exclusively contaminated blood products.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Respiratory droplet spread does not require an arthropod vector between human hosts.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl presents with a low-grade fever and a tender, enlarged lymph node in her right axilla. Two weeks earlier she developed a small papule on her right forearm after playing with a new kitten. She is otherwise healthy. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three months of doxycycline plus erythromycin

explanation.summary: Cat scratch disease in an immunocompetent patient is treated first-line with the macrolide azithromycin.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is cat scratch disease from B. henselae, presenting with a low-grade fever, an inoculation papule (3-10 days), and regional lymphadenopathy (1-3 weeks) in an axillary node after a kitten scratch. In otherwise healthy individuals, first-line therapy is a short course of the macrolide azithromycin, which helps accelerate resolution of the lymphadenitis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Intravenous gentamicin is reserved for severe plague and tularemia, not uncomplicated cat scratch disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymph node aspiration is not recommended for cases of cat scratch disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin V does not provide appropriate coverage for B. henselae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolonged doxycycline or erythromycin is used for bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, not cat scratch disease in a healthy child.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: Public health officials list Francisella tularensis as a potential agent of bioterrorism. Which of the following properties of F. tularensis most contributes to this concern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An extremely low infectious dose, as few as 10-50 bacteria

choices.label: B
choices.text: An infectious dose of 1000-2000 organisms, similar to influenza A

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resistance to all aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones

explanation.summary: F. tularensis can infect with a very small inoculum and can be aerosolized, making it a bioterrorism concern.
explanation.whyCorrect: A very small number of F. tularensis bacteria are needed to cause infection, as low as 10-50 bacteria. It can be aerosolized (for example, by skinning a rabbit) and could be aerosolized for weaponization, which is why it is considered an agent of bioterrorism.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An infectious dose of 1000-2000 organisms describes influenza A virus (ID50), not F. tularensis, whose dose is far lower.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Unlike pneumonic plague, there is no significant person-to-person transmission of tularemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: F. tularensis can readily be aerosolized, which is precisely part of the weaponization concern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: F. tularensis is treatable with aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones; it is not pan-resistant.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A pathologist is asked to distinguish bacillary angiomatosis from Kaposi sarcoma in an immunocompromised patient with red-purple skin lesions. Which of the following findings would most strongly favor bacillary angiomatosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of any identifiable bacteria on tissue stains

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lesions that occur only in immunocompetent hosts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Painless lesions that do not bleed with lymphocytic infiltrates

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tender lesions that bleed easily with neutrophilic infiltrates

explanation.summary: Bacillary angiomatosis lesions are tender, bleed easily, and show neutrophilic infiltrates, unlike Kaposi sarcoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The skin nodules of bacillary angiomatosis can resemble Kaposi sarcoma, but they are distinguished by their lesions: BA lesions are tender, bleed easily, and have neutrophilic infiltrates. BA is caused by the gram-negative bacillus B. henselae.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BA is caused by a gram-negative bacillus that can be demonstrated in tissue; absence of bacteria would argue against it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both bacillary angiomatosis and Kaposi sarcoma occur in severely immunocompromised patients, so this does not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Painless lesions that do not bleed and show lymphocytic infiltrates describe Kaposi sarcoma, not bacillary angiomatosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-8 positivity indicates Kaposi sarcoma, which is caused by that virus rather than B. henselae.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A public health officer is counseling residents of a flood-affected tropical region on how to reduce their risk of acquiring Leptospira infection. Which of the following measures is most effective in preventing human infection?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Practicing safe sex with barrier protection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets at night

choices.label: D
choices.text: Using insect repellent on exposed skin regularly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wearing gloves when handling raw poultry and meat

explanation.summary: Leptospira spreads through water, soil, or food contaminated with the urine of infected animals, so avoiding contaminated freshwater is the key preventive measure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transmission occurs when people are exposed directly or indirectly to the urine or body fluids of infected animals, often via contaminated water during flooding. The bacteria enter through skin, small cuts, or mucous membranes, so avoiding potentially contaminated freshwater (and wearing shoes) is the most effective prevention.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Person-to-person transmission of Leptospira is rare, so safe sex is not a relevant preventive measure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bed nets prevent mosquito-borne disease such as lymphatic filariasis, not water-borne leptospirosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leptospirosis is not insect-borne, so insect repellent does not prevent it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Handling poultry is not a described route of transmission for Leptospira.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man returns from a camping trip during which he waded through a flooded river. He presents with sudden onset of high fever, severe myalgia especially in the calves, headache, and red eyes without discharge. Laboratory tests reveal mild jaundice and elevated liver enzymes. Which of the following infections is most consistent with this presentation?

explanation.summary: Acute febrile illness with calf myalgia, conjunctival suffusion, and jaundice after freshwater exposure points to leptospirosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leptospirosis follows exposure to contaminated freshwater and produces fever, myalgia (especially in the calves and lower back), headache, and photophobia with conjunctival suffusion (red eyes without purulent discharge). Progression to jaundice and hepatic involvement reflects more severe disease, and L. interrogans causes the majority of clinical cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chikungunya is an arbovirus causing acute fever with prominent arthralgia, not calf myalgia with jaundice and freshwater exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dengue is an arbovirus causing febrile illness with rash and should be considered in the differential, but it does not classically cause conjunctival suffusion with jaundice from freshwater exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: W. bancrofti causes chronic lymphedema rather than an acute febrile illness with jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zika is an arbovirus causing a mild febrile illness with rash, not this waterborne hepatic picture.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man from a tropical endemic region presents with chronic swelling of his right leg and recurrent episodes of fever. On examination, the leg shows non-pitting edema and markedly thickened skin. Which of the following infections is most consistent with this clinical presentation?

explanation.summary: Chronic lymphedema with skin thickening (elephantiasis) and recurrent fevers in an endemic region is characteristic of lymphatic filariasis from W. bancrofti.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adult W. bancrofti worms live in the lymphatic vessels and, with the host immune response, cause dilation, blockage, and destruction of lymphatics. Chronic disease from repeated infection produces lymphedema and elephantiasis (thickening and fibrosis of the skin and subcutaneous tissue), often with recurrent acute inflammatory episodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chikungunya is an arbovirus causing acute fever and arthralgia, not chronic lymphedema.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dengue is an arbovirus causing acute febrile illness, not chronic limb swelling with thickened skin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leptospira causes acute febrile illness with myalgia and jaundice, not chronic elephantiasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zika is an arbovirus causing a mild acute febrile illness, not progressive lymphatic damage.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman is hospitalized with severe leptospirosis complicated by jaundice and acute kidney injury. Which of the following is the drug of choice for her treatment?

explanation.summary: Doxycycline remains the drug of choice for severe, hospitalized leptospirosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibiotics shorten disease duration, reduce urinary shedding, and prevent complications. For hospitalized patients with severe disease, doxycycline is still the drug of choice, with penicillin or ceftriaxone as alternatives.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azithromycin is an alternative for outpatients with mild disease, not the drug of choice for severe leptospirosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ceftriaxone is also only an alternative to doxycycline in severe disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diethylcarbamazine treats lymphatic filariasis (W. bancrofti), not leptospirosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillin is listed only as an alternative to doxycycline in severe disease.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is diagnosed with early lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti. Which of the following medications is preferred for early treatment?

explanation.summary: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is the preferred medication for early treatment of W. bancrofti.
explanation.whyCorrect: DEC, a piperazine derivative, is a potent microfilaricidal and macrofilaricidal agent active against W. bancrofti and is the preferred medication for early treatment. Because early lymphatic changes may be reversible, all patients with lymphatic filariasis are treated regardless of symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albendazole is an alternative agent and is used for advanced cases, not the preferred early treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxycycline is an alternative regimen and is not typically used for early treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ivermectin is used, often yearly with albendazole, to manage advanced disease rather than as preferred early treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Praziquantel is not effective against W. bancrofti.

questions.stem: A microbiology instructor describes a bacterium that causes a waterborne febrile illness and whose curved organism resembles a question mark under electron microscopy. Which of the following morphologies best describes Leptospira spp.?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gram-negative curved rods with a single polar flagellum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thin, tightly coiled spirochetes with hooked ends

explanation.summary: Leptospira are thin, tightly coiled, highly motile spirochetes with hooked ends.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leptospira spp. are coiled, thin, highly motile spirochetes with hooked ends and two periplasmic flagella, giving a question mark-like appearance. Although they have an outer membrane and are considered gram-negative, they stain poorly with Gram stain and are difficult to visualize with light microscopy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gram-negative curved rods with polar flagella describes organisms such as Vibrio, not Leptospira.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gram-negative diplococci describes organisms such as Neisseria, not a coiled spirochete.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gram-positive cocci in clusters describes staphylococci, not a spirochete.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spore-forming gram-positive rods describe organisms such as Clostridium or Bacillus, not Leptospira.

questions.stem: A physician suspects lymphatic filariasis and orders a peripheral blood smear to detect microfilariae of Wuchereria bancrofti. To maximize the yield of the smear, when should the blood sample be collected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At any time of day, since timing does not matter

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the early morning while fasting

explanation.summary: Microfilariae of W. bancrofti are nocturnal, so blood for a smear should be collected at night (10 PM to 2 AM).
explanation.whyCorrect: The most straightforward way to identify W. bancrofti is a peripheral blood smear stained with Giemsa or hematoxylin-and-eosin. Because the microfilariae are nocturnal and enter the blood predominantly at night, collecting the sample between 10 PM and 2 AM yields better results.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Timing does matter for the blood smear; only antigen detection can be collected any time because antigens circulate throughout the day.
whyWrongByChoice.B: At midday the microfilariae are not at their peak in the blood, lowering smear yield.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Timing sampling to a mosquito bite is not how microfilaremia is detected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Early-morning fasting collection does not coincide with the nocturnal peak of microfilariae.

questions.stem: An elderly man with leptospirosis deteriorates and develops jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage. This severe icterohemorrhagic form of leptospirosis is best known by which of the following names?

explanation.summary: Severe leptospirosis with jaundice, kidney injury, and hemorrhage is called Weil disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Severe leptospirosis is sometimes referred to as Weil disease or icterohemorrhagic leptospirosis and is associated with children, the elderly, and patients with pre-existing conditions. Shock, hemorrhage, jaundice, and acute kidney injury are common in severe cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjunctival suffusion is a mild sign of leptospirosis, not the severe icterohemorrhagic form.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Elephantiasis is a chronic complication of lymphatic filariasis, not severe leptospirosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The filarial dance sign is an ultrasound finding of moving worms in filariasis, not a leptospirosis syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia is a hypersensitivity reaction seen in lymphatic filariasis, not a form of leptospirosis.

questions.stem: A patient in a region where dengue and chikungunya are endemic presents with an undifferentiated febrile illness, and leptospirosis is suspected. Given the difficulty of culturing the organism and the limitations of serology, which of the following is the preferred method to confirm the diagnosis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Light microscopy of a wet mount

explanation.summary: PCR is the preferred confirmatory test for leptospirosis because culture is difficult and serology is limited.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cultures of Leptospira are time consuming and difficult and are not used for routine diagnosis, and serology has limitations. Because of these constraints, PCR (nucleic acid amplification) is the preferred method of confirming a diagnosis, and leptospirosis should always be considered in the differential in arbovirus-endemic areas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single antibody titer is limited; titers take up to 2 weeks to rise and prior exposure can elevate them, so paired titers are needed rather than one acute sample.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cultures of Leptospira are time consuming and difficult and are not employed in routine diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leptospira stain poorly with Gram stain and are difficult to visualize, so Gram stain is not confirmatory.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thin cells are difficult to visualize under a light microscope, making wet-mount microscopy unreliable.

questions.stem: A patient with lymphatic filariasis develops a cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath resembling asthma. Laboratory studies show marked eosinophilia and elevated IgE levels. Which of the following best explains this presentation?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute kidney injury from the parasitic infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secondary bacterial cellulitis of the limb

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weil disease with jaundice and renal failure

explanation.summary: Asthma-like symptoms with eosinophilia and elevated IgE in filariasis reflect tropical pulmonary eosinophilia, a hypersensitivity reaction to microfilariae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some patients in the acute phase develop a hypersensitivity reaction to microfilariae in the blood known as tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE). This produces asthma-like symptoms including coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath, with laboratory findings of eosinophilia and elevated IgE.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute kidney injury is a feature of severe leptospirosis, not this eosinophilic respiratory reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydrocele is scrotal swelling from chronic lymphatic obstruction, not a pulmonary hypersensitivity syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secondary bacterial cellulitis complicates chronic lymphedema but does not cause asthma-like symptoms with eosinophilia and elevated IgE.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Weil disease is a severe form of leptospirosis, not a manifestation of lymphatic filariasis.

questions.stem: A patient with mild leptospirosis is treated as an outpatient with doxycycline. By which of the following mechanisms does doxycycline exert its antibacterial effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis

explanation.summary: Doxycycline is a tetracycline that inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit.
explanation.whyCorrect: For outpatients with mild leptospirosis, treatment is similar to that for rickettsia, and doxycycline (a tetracycline and 30S protein synthesis inhibitor) is the go-to agent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cell wall synthesis inhibition describes beta-lactams such as penicillin, not a tetracycline.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA gyrase inhibition describes fluoroquinolones, not doxycycline.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate synthesis inhibition describes sulfonamides, not doxycycline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibition of the 50S subunit describes macrolides such as azithromycin, the alternative agent, not doxycycline.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing how Wuchereria bancrofti is transmitted to humans. Through which of the following vectors is W. bancrofti predominantly transmitted?

explanation.summary: W. bancrofti is a nematode transmitted by the bites of female mosquitoes.
explanation.whyCorrect: W. bancrofti is a nematode (roundworm) transmitted via the bites of female mosquitoes; depending on the region it is predominantly carried by Culex, Anopheles, or Aedes spp. Mosquito control with treated bed nets, repellents, and insecticide spraying reduces transmission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blackflies transmit Onchocerca, a different filarial nematode, not W. bancrofti.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ixodes ticks transmit spirochetes such as Borrelia, not W. bancrofti.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sandflies transmit other pathogens (such as Leishmania), not W. bancrofti.
